You previously formulated the following research problem for the target paper.

Research problem: In MVFA, only the segmentation adapters produce anomaly maps, and they are trained exclusively with Dice and Focal losses on pixel masks from three BMAD datasets (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC), while the image-labelled datasets (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS) only ever train the detection adapters. Can the segmentation adapters instead be trained from image-level labels alone — through a multiple-instance objective on each level's segmentation-branch patch-to-text similarity map (primary operator: top-k mean of patch anomaly probabilities, so that an abnormal image must contain a few highly abnormal patches and a normal image none) applied to all five source datasets with masks discarded — and how much of the mask-supervised zero-shot localisation (pixel-level AUROC and PRO) and detection (image-level AUROC) on the held-out modality does this retain? The comparison is mask-supervised MVFA versus image-label-supervised MVFA, both trained and model-selected under the shared protocol.
Rationale: Limitation G3, corrected against the released code, shows that MVFA's localisation depends entirely on dense expert masks from three datasets, and G4 shows that even its few-shot mode needs K abnormal images with masks. Image-level labels are cheap and already available for every BMAD dataset, but MVFA never uses them to teach the segmentation branch where anomalies are. The related literature does not answer whether text-anchored patch similarities in a multi-level CLIP adapter can learn localisation from weak labels: MedSAD-CLIP, MLCA and MadCLIP keep pixel or labelled abnormal supervision, AnoCLIP and SAA+ avoid training altogether, and MedCLIP-SAMv2 uses weak supervision only for a separate segmentation model. The question is narrow — it changes the training signal of one branch — and directly implementable by replacing the seg_loss term in the public training script; a negative result still quantifies what masks are worth for cross-modality localisation. Under the shared protocol, both variants are selected on a source-modality validation split rather than on the target test set, so the comparison is not biased in favour of either.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G3. Localisation supervision requires dense masks: MVFA trains two branches. The detection (classification) adapters receive an image-level BCE loss on every source image, including the three BMAD datasets that have no masks (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS). The segmentation adapters, which produce the anomaly maps, are trained only with Dice and Focal losses on pixel-level masks, i.e. only on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC. Localisation therefore depends entirely on dense expert masks from three datasets; no image-level, sparse or normal-only supervision of the segmentation branch is formulated.
- G4. The few-shot setting needs labelled abnormal images with masks and is evaluated on one draw: In the released code, 'K-shot' means K normal AND K abnormal images, the abnormal ones with pixel masks, both drawn from BMAD's valid/ split; the adapters are fine-tuned on them per target task. Clinical few-shot supervision may instead contain only normal or unlabelled images, which the method does not support. Only one fixed draw per dataset is provided. Training time and compute for the per-task fine-tuning are not reported.

Problem: Can MVFA's segmentation adapters — which today learn localisation only from pixel masks of BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC — learn transferable localisation from image-level labels alone? We replace the Dice and Focal seg_loss with a multiple-instance objective on the segmentation-branch patch-to-text similarity map at each of the four levels (primary operator: mean of the top 2% of patch anomaly probabilities; max and mean pooling as ablations) and train on all five source datasets with masks discarded. Hypothesis: because each patch is scored against a shared text anchor, image-level supervision forces patch-level anomaly evidence to align with the text 'abnormal' direction, so localisation learned this way transfers to the unseen modality and retains at least 80% of the mask-supervised pixel-level AUROC. Outcomes on the held-out modality: pixel-level AUROC and PRO, image-level AUROC, the per-level localisation quality (which levels produce useful maps), and a label-budget curve comparing image-labelled training on all datasets with mask-supervised training on 10-100% of the masked images.

Rationale: Reviewers rated relevance and feasibility highest and asked for an explicit, distinctive hypothesis, the value of k, the level at which the loss applies, and a decision-relevant label-budget view. The hypothesis now states what is specific to the vision-language setting: localisation through text-anchored patch similarities rather than class-activation maps, tested across modalities. The operator is fixed (top 2%) and applied at all four levels with a per-level analysis. The label-budget curve answers the practical question a site faces — whether many cheaply labelled images can substitute for few masked ones. The change remains a single loss term in the public training script, evaluated under the shared protocol with source-validation model selection.
